candidate.answerReason: The 5.0 and 4.8 m/s runners first meet again after 2500 seconds. At that time all three have completed whole numbers of laps, so this is also their first simultaneous reunion.

methods.label: Use the closest pair of speeds
methods.explanation:
For all three runners to meet, the runners traveling at \(5.0\) and \(4.8\) meters per second must meet. Two runners on this track occupy the same point when their traveled distances differ by a whole number of \(500\)-meter laps.

The faster runner gains on the other at \(5.0-4.8=0.2\) meters per second. Their first meeting after the start occurs when that gain reaches one lap, after
\[
\frac{500}{0.2}=2500\text{ seconds}.
\]
Thus all three cannot meet earlier. In \(2500\) seconds, their distances are
\[
4.4(2500)=11000,
\quad 4.8(2500)=12000,
\quad 5.0(2500)=12500
\]
meters. These are respectively \(22\), \(24\), and \(25\) complete laps, so all three are together at the starting point. They run for \(\boxed{2500}\) seconds, choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
methods.levelReason: Relative speed, distance divided by speed, and whole-lap reasoning are elementary travel-problem tools within AMC 10.

candidate.annotationRationale: The target is a circular-track catch-up problem. Distance equals speed times time supports both the necessary pairwise meeting condition and the final check. The written method needs neither an LCM calculation nor a full linear-equation modeling workflow.

review.mathematicalCheck: The closest-speed pair first reunites after \(500/0.2=2500\) seconds, ruling out any earlier triple reunion. At that time the runners complete 22, 24, and 25 laps, proving sufficiency.
